articles.author: Jason “Jman” Mckay
articles.description:
Enforcing agent safety in the tool layer, not the system prompt.
Drawn from a personal agentic system ("Vantage") I built and run daily.
Most agent "guardrails" are sentences. Somewhere in a system prompt there is a line like "Never delete files without asking" or "Do not send email on the user's behalf." The line is polite, it is well-intentioned, and it is not a control. It is a request addressed to a probabilistic text generator, evaluated anew on every turn, competing with everything else in the context window. The day it loses that competition is the day you find out your safety model was a suggestion.
I want to argue a narrower and more useful position than "prompts are unreliable," which everyone already knows. The position is: the boundary between what an agent may suggest and what…
articles.title: The permission you can't prompt away

The opposite failure is premature architecture: five linked sheets, IMPORTRANGE across files, and a Notion hub for a workflow that still fits on one screen.
This post is a decision guide for when to keep one sheet and when to split—aimed at Excel / Google Sheets templates (with a short Notion parallel) for people who run their own work.
Ask: what is one complete record?
One expense line
One content piece
One applicant
One weekly review row
If you can’t name the atomic unit, you aren’t ready to split. You’re still discovering the workflow. Stay on one sheet…
articles.title: One Sheet vs Linked Sheets: When to Break Up a Solo-Operator Template

articles.description:
CrowdSec vs Fail2Ban vs CSF: Choosing Intrusion Prevention for Linux Servers


A Linux server with a public IP address can start receiving SSH brute-force attempts, automated port scans, and suspicious login requests soon after deployment.
A firewall controls which connections are allowed. But what happens when an IP address repeatedly attempts to log in through an exposed SSH service?
That's where intrusion prevention tools help. They detect suspicious behavior and can block offending IP addresses before repeated attempts become a bigger problem.
Three commonly discussed options are CrowdSec, Fail2Ban, and CSF (ConfigServer Security & Firewall). Here's how they differ and when to consider each one.
Fail2Ban monitors logs or the systemd journal for patterns such as repeated failed logins. …
articles.title: CrowdSec vs Fail2Ban vs CSF: Choosing Intrusion Prevention for Linux Servers

articles.description:
A Windows scheduled-task saga, and the fix that wasn't where the flag was.
A debugging story from my own machine, with a lesson that outlived the bug.
The symptom was absurd enough to feel like a prank. Every so often — no pattern I could see at first — a black terminal window would snap open on my desktop, hold focus for a second or two, and vanish. Mid-sentence, mid-click, it didn't matter: the window would steal the foreground, eat a keystroke or two, and be gone before I could read what was in it. A ghost with a short attention span.
These were my own scheduled tasks. Housekeeping jobs — snapshots, log collectors, a daily brief — all PowerShell, all registered by me, and every one of them launched with the flag that is supposed to make exactly this not happen:
powershell.exe -WindowSty…

articles.author: Florient DOGBE
articles.description:
Signing a container image is a ten-minute task. Making your cluster refuse anything unsigned is the part most teams never finish. The result is a supply chain security story that looks great in a slide deck and provides exactly zero protection at runtime: the signatures exist in the registry, nobody checks them, and a kubectl run with an arbitrary image from Docker Hub still lands in production.
This article builds the full chain end to end: keyless OIDC signing in CI, a CycloneDX SBOM attestation attached to the image, and a Kyverno verifyImages policy that fails closed on an OpenShift or Kubernetes cluster. Every step is verifiable from a terminal.
A Cosign signature is just another OCI artifact pushed next to your image (historically a sha256-<digest>.sig tag, now also discoverable thro…
articles.title: Sign and Verify Container Images with Cosign and an Admission Policy That Actually Blocks

Firefox has a built-in screenshot tool that most people don't know about. Here's what it does, where it is, and when to use it over external tools.

Userscripts are JavaScript snippets that run on specific websites. Firefox supports them via the Tampermonkey or Violentmonkey extensions. Here's a practical guide.
A userscript runs after a page loads and can:
Modify page content (add/remove/change elements)
Inject custom CSS styling
Add buttons or functionality
Automate repetitive actions
Remove annoyances (cookie banners, overlays)
They're like micro-extensions, but easier to write and share as single files.
Install Violentmonkey (open source, recommended) or Tampermonkey from AMO:
Violentmonkey — fully open source
Tampermonkey — more widely used, partly closed source
Both work similarly. Userscripts are managed via the extension's dashboard.

articles.author: Florient DOGBE
articles.description:
Every OpenShift cluster ships with at least two ways to expose an HTTP service, and since 4.14 there is a third. Route is the native OpenShift object, Ingress is the portable Kubernetes one, and the Gateway API is the upstream replacement for Ingress — implemented on OpenShift by an Istio-based gateway controller managed by the Cluster Ingress Operator.
This is not a cosmetic choice. The abstraction you pick determines where TLS is terminated, which timeouts you can tune, whether you can do header manipulation or traffic splitting without a sidecar hack, and which metrics you will have during an incident at 3 a.m. This article compares the three on concrete limits, then walks through migrating a production Route loaded with HAProxy annotations to a Gateway API HTTPRoute with re-encrypt TLS…
articles.title: Routes, Ingress or Gateway API on OpenShift 4: Which to Choose and How to Migrate

articles.description:
A few weeks ago I shipped AgeDart, a game about one simple question: how old does this person look?
You see real faces (everyone who posts a photo opted in) and throw a dart at the age you think. The closer you land, the more points. And if you post your own selfie, strangers around the world guess your age and you get a verdict broken down by country, age group and gender.

It has to cost almost nothing while nobody plays it.
It must not fall over (or bankrupt me) if a video goes viral.
This post is about how those two constraints shaped the architecture. The app is Flutter (Android first, iOS in review), the backend is Firebase.
